requirement: Users sign in and sign out; sessions expire (see SEC-02).

Support four roles: Administrator, Building Manager, Resident (Tenant or Owner), Technician. Role assignments are scoped: managers to buildings; technicians to buildings (and categories, if modelled); residents to units through ownership, lease or household membership.

Keep the person (identity and contact data), the user account and the role assignments separate. A person may hold several roles; a person may exist without an account (for example a household member).

No public self-registration. Administrators invite or create users of any role; Building Managers invite residents of their buildings. Administrators assign and revoke roles and deactivate accounts. Accounts are never hard-deleted; their history remains.
Enforce object-level authorization on every API operation: access depends on the role and the relationship to the resource (for example a resident can read a lease only if they are a party to it).
The interface adapts to the role (navigation, actions), but the API is always the enforcement point.
Profile page with contact details, notification preferences and password change (or a link to the identity provider).
Multi-factor authentication or passkeys.

Manage buildings (name, address, contact, status), floors (level, label), units (number, type — apartment, commercial, storage or parking — area in m², rooms, floor) and common areas (stairwell, basement, elevator, roof and similar).

A unit's status combines occupancy (Occupied or Vacant, derived from the M3 occupancy records) and an operational state: Open issue (unit has an active work order, see M4), Under maintenance (a work order for the unit is In Progress), Unavailable (set by a manager, with a reason) or Normal. Derived states are calculated, never set by hand. When several apply the map shows the most severe: Unavailable, then Under maintenance, then Open issue.

Each floor has a layout stored as data (for example rectangles or polygons with coordinates for each unit and common area, in JSON or relational form). Seed at least two buildings with different layouts. A layout editor MAY be provided; importing layouts from JSON is acceptable.

Interactive 2D floor map rendered from layout and live status data (SVG or Canvas): choose building and floor; units drawn from the layout; status shown with colour AND a pattern, icon or label (never colour alone); a legend; filter or highlight by status; tooltip on hover and focus; click or Enter opens the unit detail page.

Map accessibility: every unit is reachable by keyboard and has an accessible name (example: "Unit 4B, occupied, 1 open issue"). Provide an equivalent list or table view with the same data and filters.
Role-aware map data: residents see their building without other residents' personal data; managers see full detail for their buildings; technicians see units with assigned work highlighted.
Unit detail page: attributes, occupancy and current lease (if authorized), open and past work orders, meters and recent readings, recent statements (if authorized), and history.
The map reflects changes without a full page reload: refetch on focus or on an interval in Core; real-time push is FE-A03 and BE-A04.
Zoom and pan, minimap, print view.
Manage persons (owners, tenants, household members) with minimal personal data. Document why each personal field is needed (data minimization, SEC-13).
Ownership records link units to one or more owners with start and end dates (an ownership share MAY be recorded).

Lease lifecycle: Draft → Active (a manager activates; activation checks M3-04) → Ended (scheduled job after the end date, M3-06); Draft → Cancelled; Active → Terminated (early, with a reason and an effective date). A lease records unit, tenant(s), start and end dates, monthly rent and currency, deposit and notes. A renewal creates a new Draft lease linked to the previous one.
No overlapping active leases for the same unit. Enforce in the database or in a transaction that is safe under concurrent requests, and prove it with a test.
Occupancy history per unit — who lived there, when, in what capacity — derived from ownership, lease and household records.
A scheduled job flags leases ending within 30 days (notifying the manager and the tenant once per lease) and moves leases past their end date to Ended.
Managers manage leases in their buildings; residents read their own leases; technicians have no access to leases.
Attach a signed lease document (PDF) following the safe-upload rules in SEC-07.

Residents (and managers on their behalf) submit requests with location (unit or common area), category (Plumbing, Electrical, Heating, Elevator, Cleaning, Other), priority (Low, Normal, High, Emergency), description and up to three photos (validated type and size, for example JPEG, PNG or WebP, up to 5 MB each).
Implement the work-order state machine in the transition table and diagram below.
The API rejects invalid transitions with a domain error (ProblemDetails, HTTP 409 or 422). Every allowed and forbidden transition is tested for each role.

A configurable SLA policy (Administrator) sets the target resolution time per priority — for example Emergency 4 hours, High 24 hours, Normal 3 days, Low 7 days. The due date is calculated at submission (submission time + target) and recalculated if the manager changes the priority during triage. Work orders show due soon (less than 25% of the target time left) and overdue indicators.
Work can be assigned only to technicians eligible for the building (and category, if modelled). Reassignment keeps the history.
Two comment channels: resident-visible comments and internal work notes (managers and technicians only), separated by the API — not just hidden in the interface.
A complete status history (who, when, from → to, reason) and audit records.
A technician work queue with filters (status, priority, due date) and a work-order detail view with quick status actions.
Notifications to the reporter on every status change (internal notes are never included), and to managers on new High or Emergency requests and on SLA breaches.
An SLA escalation job flags overdue work orders and notifies the manager exactly once per breach (idempotent).
An auto-close job closes Resolved work orders after 7 days without a reopen.
A Kanban board for managers and technicians with drag-and-drop status changes and a keyboard-accessible alternative.
The reporter confirms the resolution and MAY rate the service from 1 to 5.
Record labour time and parts used.

Manage meters: utility type (cold water, hot water, electricity, gas, heating), serial number, scope (a specific unit, or the building/common areas), unit of measure (for example m³, kWh), installation date, removal date.
At most one reading per meter per billing period. Residents submit readings for meters of their own unit (a self-reading, may include a photo). Building Managers can also submit readings.

A new reading cannot be lower than the previous one unless a meter-replacement record exists. Plausibility check: consumption above a configurable threshold is flagged for manager review (suggested example: 3× the unit's recent average). Correcting a reading requires a reason; every correction is audited.
Tariffs per building and per utility, with an effective date range, a price per unit consumed and a currency.

Common building expenses per building and billing period (cleaning, elevator maintenance, common-area electricity, administration fees). Each has an allocation rule: by unit area (m²), by number of occupants, equally per unit, or by consumption. Implement at least two rules.

Monthly billing run per building and billing period: Preview → Approve → Issue (MAY: approve and issue combined in one action). Statement content = individual consumption × applicable tariff + the unit's allocated share of every common expense. Re-running a preview replaces the existing preview (idempotent; no duplicate lines). Every statement has a due date, configurable per building, default 30 days after issuance. Issued statements are immutable; corrections use adjustment lines or credit notes, each with a reason.

Exact money: decimal types only, never floating point. Allocation is deterministic and the allocated amounts sum exactly to the source amount. Default rule: calculate at full precision; round each line to 2 decimal places, half-away-from-zero; assign leftover cents to the units with the largest fractional remainders. MAY use another documented rule that is still exact and deterministic.

Statement state machine: Draft → Issued; Issued → Partially Paid; Partially Paid → Paid; Issued → Paid (full settlement); Issued → Overdue; Partially Paid → Overdue; Overdue → Paid (remaining balance settled); Issued → Cancelled (Building Manager, with a reason). A scheduled job moves eligible statements to Overdue after the due date; a partially paid statement past its due date stays Overdue until fully settled.

Payments are simulated (no real funds). Managers record amount, payment date, method and reference. MAY: residents get a "Pay (simulation)" action through a fake payment-provider abstraction. Partial payments supported; a payment cannot exceed the outstanding balance; applying a payment is idempotent (idempotency key or unique payment reference).
Residents view their statements, line details, current outstanding balance, payment history and a consumption chart for the previous 12 months.
A configurable reminder job notifies residents who have not submitted required readings a set number of days before the billing period closes.
Late fees using a configurable daily rate.

Building Managers create announcements for assigned buildings; Administrators for all. Fields: title; rich-text body (sanitized on the server); category (Outage, Maintenance, Meeting, General, Urgent); audience targeting by building, floor and role; publish time; expiry time; pinned flag.
Lifecycle: Draft → Scheduled → Published → Expired → Archived. Immediate publishing skips Scheduled. Scheduled publishing and expiry are performed by scheduled jobs.
Residents and Technicians see only announcements targeted to them. The list supports filtering and pagination.

In-app notification centre for event-driven notifications about work orders, statements, leases, announcements and meter readings: unread-count badge, mark as read, mark as unread, mark all as read, paginated history.
A notification is created reliably together with the business change that triggered it: either in the same transaction, or via a transactional outbox (BE-A03).
Notification preferences per category; critical categories cannot be disabled.
Aggregate "seen by" counts for announcements. Must not expose who read it or individual reading behaviour.
Email or SMS through a provider abstraction. If implemented: sandbox services only (for example a local SMTP catcher); the application MUST keep working when the provider is unavailable.

Audit records for important changes: sign-in events, role changes, leases, work-order transitions, meter readings and corrections, billing runs, statements, payments, announcements. Each record captures: actor, UTC timestamp, entity type, entity ID, action, before/after values (or a structured change set), outcome (Success or Failure), correlation ID.
Audit records are append-only from the application's perspective: no path to update or delete. Administrators see all records; Building Managers only records relating to their assigned buildings.
Audit viewer with entity, actor, action and date-range filters and server-side pagination.
Role dashboards (contents below).
At least one CSV export (example: outstanding balances per unit). Every export enforces authorization and never exposes records outside the user's scope.
Every chart has an accessible alternative (a textual summary or a data table with the same information).
Statements as PDF.
Every list that can become large uses server-side pagination; data-heavy lists support search, filtering and sorting (units, persons, work orders, statements, audit records are named explicitly).
Every data view handles all four states: loading, empty, error, success.
Validation on both client and server, with consistent field-level messages across the two layers.
Dates and times stored in UTC, displayed in the user's time zone (default Europe/Bucharest); the API uses ISO 8601.
Money stored as decimals; every amount has an explicit currency code (default RON); consistent formatting everywhere.
Business records that carry history are archived or deactivated, not deleted. Hard deletion only where documented (certain drafts; records removed for a valid privacy erasure).
Destructive or irreversible actions require confirmation; every important action gives clear feedback.

Synthetic, reproducible, realistic seed data: at least 2 buildings, 60 units, 100 persons, 12 months of meter readings, 12 months of statements, 300 work orders spread across all work-order states. Documented demo accounts for every role. Must include Aurora Residence, unit 4B, the scenario personas, and all data needed to replay Scenarios A and B.
English for interface text, code, code comments, documentation, commit messages, PRs and work items. Bilingual English/Romanian is optional extension X6, not Core.
Every participant owns at least one package and is its primary author. Ownership is recorded in the Week-1 Team Charter and in CODEOWNERS (or the Azure DevOps equivalent).
Every participant records at least 40 hours of evidenced work (PRC-06/07). Work should be balanced across the team; any large imbalance is explained in the retrospective.
Ownership must not become isolation: every participant reviews pull requests outside their own track each week and can explain the complete end-to-end architecture.
Every participant delivers at least one vertical slice spanning interface → API → database.
If a participant leaves, the team notifies the jury within one week. The jury adjusts the Advanced-package requirement. Merged work stays credited to its original author.
Solo participation needs the jury's written approval; the solo participant delivers the two-person-team scope and obtains PR reviews from a review buddy on another team.
React 19.2+ with Next.js 16+ (App Router) or TanStack Start 1.x. TypeScript strict mode. Linter and formatter run in CI. Next.js 15 or earlier is not permitted as the starting version.
evidence: ADR for the framework choice; repo config showing framework/version, strict TS, lint, format

requirement: Define the rendering strategy for every route (static/prerendered, SSR, streaming SSR, CSR) plus server/client component boundaries where supported. Include at least 1 personalized SSR route, 1 cached or prerendered route, and 1 client-rendered interactive area (the map).
evidence: Rendering Strategy Table in `docs/architecture` with a reason for every route

requirement: Role-specific layouts and navigation. Protected routes; redirect unauthenticated/unauthorized users. Dedicated 403, 404 and 500 pages.
evidence: Code; E2E smoke test for navigation and access by role

requirement: Typed API client (SHOULD be generated from the OpenAPI document, for example with Kiota or openapi-typescript). Server-state caching and revalidation (for example TanStack Query or framework caching). Every view supports loading, empty, error and success states. Access tokens are never stored in browser storage.
evidence: Code; screenshots of the four states

requirement: Forms via React 19 Actions (`useActionState`, `useFormStatus`) or a suitable form library. Client validation mirrors server rules (a shared validation schema SHOULD be used). Map server ProblemDetails validation errors to individual fields; move focus to the first invalid field; show pending/submission states.

Optimistic UI for at least 2 low-risk interactions (for example mark a notification read, add a comment) using `useOptimistic` or cache-level updates. On failure roll back and give clear feedback. Document where optimistic UI was deliberately avoided (for example payments) and why.
evidence: Code; automated test or recording of the rollback/failure path

requirement: The data-driven 2D floor map from M2-04..M2-06: renders from layout and live status data; keyboard and screen-reader support; equivalent list view; role-appropriate data exposure; lazy loading.

WCAG 2.2 Level AA for core flows: semantic HTML, landmarks, labels, visible focus, sufficient contrast, status not conveyed by colour alone, accessible charts. Automated axe checks in CI; manually complete both signature scenarios with keyboard and screen reader.
Resident and technician workflows work at 360 px viewport width. Manager and administrator workflows work on desktop and tablet layouts.
Error boundaries per route or route segment. Degrade gracefully when the API or the real-time channel is unavailable; offer a retry.
Component tests for key UI (forms, floor map, status badges). Playwright E2E tests for both signature scenarios (shared with OPS). Accessibility assertions included.
Stream dashboard widgets independently behind Suspense boundaries with skeleton placeholders. Build or measure a non-streamed comparison; record TTFB and LCP for both.

Advanced caching for the chosen framework. Next.js: Cache Components, `use cache`, cache tags, post-mutation revalidation. TanStack Start: route loaders, query prefetching, hydration, invalidation. Document what is cached in browser, web server and API and how each layer is invalidated.
Live notification badge and live work-order updates via SignalR or Server-Sent Events, with reconnection, backoff, reconciliation with the client cache, and a polling fallback.

Kanban workflow with optimistic card moves. Handle version/concurrency conflicts returned as HTTP 409 or 412 with a clear refresh-or-merge experience. Keyboard-accessible alternative to drag-and-drop.
evidence: Demonstration; tests incl. conflict handling and keyboard use

requirement: Measure the three Core Web Vitals LCP, INP, CLS (Lighthouse CI or `web-vitals`). Enable the React Compiler or otherwise optimize with React Profiler evidence. Code-split heavy UI (map, charts). Before-and-after measurements.
evidence: Report in `docs/performance` with profiler and Core Web Vitals evidence

requirement: Documented reusable component library (for example Storybook with accessibility checks). Design tokens for colour, spacing and typography, used consistently. Light and dark themes.

ASP.NET Core on .NET 10 LTS (.NET 11 only after general availability and with an ADR). Choose controllers or Minimal APIs and justify it in an ADR (Minimal APIs: expect route groups, endpoint filters, `TypedResults`). Structure the solution as a modular monolith with clear module boundaries.
evidence: ADR (API style; .NET 11 if adopted); inspectable solution structure showing module boundaries

requirement: Resource-oriented HTTP API: correct verbs and status codes; consistent pagination, filtering, sorting; RFC 9457 ProblemDetails for every error; an API versioning strategy (for example `/api/v1`); 201 Created with a `Location` header on creation.
evidence: API conventions document + code demonstrating them

requirement: Generate an OpenAPI document with schemas, examples and security definitions. Interactive docs via Scalar or Swagger UI, not exposed in the Release environment. Store and version the OpenAPI file with the source.
evidence: Versioned OpenAPI file; URL of the interactive docs in a permitted environment

requirement: Authentication via ASP.NET Core Identity (cookies or bearer) or an OpenID Connect provider (for example Microsoft Entra ID or Keycloak). Role-based and policy-based authorization; resource-based authorization handlers for object-level checks; deny by default.

Request validation (built-in Minimal API validation, FluentValidation, DataAnnotations or equivalent permitted). HTTP 409 or 422 for domain-rule violations. Centralised exception handling with `IExceptionHandler`. No stack traces or internals in responses.
evidence: Code and tests for validation, domain conflicts and sanitised errors

requirement: Data access with EF Core, Dapper or the DB's official driver. Explicit transactions for multi-record operations (example: triage + assignment + history + audit + notification written atomically). Document connection-pool configuration (pool size, timeouts, DbContext pooling if used) and how each request obtains and returns a connection.

Cache at least 2 repeatedly requested reads (for example floor layouts, tariffs, dashboard aggregates) using HybridCache, `IMemoryCache` or output caching. Explicit invalidation on writes (tags allowed). Cache hits and misses observable in logs or metrics.
evidence: Caching + invalidation code; logs/metrics showing hits and misses

requirement: Implement every scheduled job required by M3-06, M4-10, M4-11, M5-08, M6-02: lease expiry, SLA escalation, work-order auto-close, overdue statements, scheduled announcement publish and expiry. Scheduler: `BackgroundService`, Hangfire, Quartz.NET or equivalent permitted. Each job idempotent, safe if run twice, logged and observable (last run and outcome).
evidence: Job code + job dashboard or logs showing runs and outcomes

requirement: Capture all audit records required by M7-01, including correlation IDs. An EF Core `SaveChanges` interceptor or database triggers agreed with the DB owner are acceptable.
evidence: Audit code + a functioning audit viewer

requirement: Separate liveness and readiness health endpoints (readiness checks the database). Structured JSON logs with correlation IDs and no sensitive data. Graceful shutdown.

Unit tests for domain rules (state machines, billing allocation, lease overlap). Integration tests against a real database (for example `WebApplicationFactory` + Testcontainers). Authorization tests generated from the roles-and-permissions matrix.

Optimistic concurrency across the whole request flow for work orders, leases and statements: ETag with `If-Match`, or explicit version fields; conflicts follow HTTP 412 or 409 semantics. Tests show stale writes cannot overwrite newer data.
evidence: Automated tests + API docs describing the concurrency contract

requirement: Distributed L2 cache for HybridCache using Valkey, Memcached or Dragonfly via an `IDistributedCache` implementation. Cache-stampede protection, documented key strategy, TTL strategy, tag-based invalidation. Load-test (k6 or Azure Load Testing); compare before/after latency percentiles and database-call counts. Reproduce a connection-pool exhaustion scenario under load, then fix it.
evidence: Report in `docs/performance`: configuration, method, before/after, percentiles, DB-call evidence, exhaustion diagnosis and fix

requirement: Transactional outbox for notifications and integration events; idempotent consumers; payment endpoints accept an `Idempotency-Key` header. Tests prove correct behaviour when a message or request is delivered more than once.
evidence: Outbox + consumer code; duplicate-delivery and payment-idempotency tests

requirement: Server-to-client push via a SignalR hub or Server-Sent Events, authorised per user and per building. Document a scale-out design (Azure SignalR Service, or a Valkey or Dragonfly backplane). Memcached is not an approved backplane (no pub/sub).
evidence: Working demo + design note on authorization and scale-out

requirement: Put notifications, file storage and the payment simulator behind provider abstractions. Timeouts, retries with jitter and circuit breakers (Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience, Polly or equivalent). Fault-injection test showing graceful degradation.
evidence: Automated tests + demo of the injected failure

requirement: Rate limiting on sign-in, password reset and other abuse-prone endpoints: HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header. OpenTelemetry traces and metrics; custom metrics for work orders created, billing-run duration, cache-hit ratio; export to a dashboard.
Document the database decision in an ADR comparing SQL and NoSQL: consistency requirements, query patterns, team skills, engine, hosting.
ERD for SQL, or a document/access-pattern model for NoSQL, covering M1–M7, with a data dictionary. SQL: 3NF where appropriate; document intentional denormalization/embedding.
Enforce integrity with SQL constraints or NoSQL schema validation/indexes. The M3-04 lease-overlap rule is protected by the database or by a concurrency-safe transaction.
Versioned migrations, validated automatically in CI against a disposable DB; reproducible synthetic seed data (PX-08); documented migration naming and review rules.
Define indexes for the 10 most important query patterns and justify them; at least 2 with before/after execution plans.
Programmable DB objects. SQL: at least 2 stored procedures/functions, 1 view and 1 trigger, all automatically tested. NoSQL: the equivalents in the table below.
Identify operations that need atomicity; document the chosen isolation level and rationale, with implementation and tests.
Backup policy and a restore drill into a fresh environment, validated with counts/checksums plus an application smoke test.
Least-privilege application login (never DB owner/admin); credentials from a secret store; TLS where supported. A separate migration identity SHOULD be used.
Temporal/history capability for leases, tariffs and statements, including "as of" queries. SQL Server/Azure SQL: system-versioned tables; PostgreSQL: trigger-maintained history tables.
Reporting layer: materialized/indexed views or summary tables refreshed by a job, plus window-function trends (for example monthly consumption, arrears buckets).
Performance lab with at least 1,000,000 meter readings and 100,000 work orders: inspect plans, tune indexes, compare offset vs keyset pagination, document conclusions.
Reproduce and correct a race condition (constraints/isolation/locking) and investigate one deadlock scenario.
Demonstrate a zero-downtime expand-and-contract schema change through the pipeline, with a rollback or forward-fix strategy.
Privacy/retention: anonymization of former residents while preserving financial and audit integrity; a retention job for expired data.
Private GitHub or Azure DevOps repo; protection on `main` and `preview`; CODEOWNERS; PR and work-item templates; `.editorconfig`; `.gitignore`; jury read access by end of Week 1.
GitHub Projects / Azure Boards backlog with module epics, stories with acceptance criteria, tasks, weekly iterations, linked PRs/work items, effort-tracking fields.

CI for PRs targeting `preview` and `main`: restore, build, lint/analyzers, unit/integration tests, migration validation against an ephemeral DB, frontend build/tests, container build — all as required status checks. Dependency caching expected.

Multi-stage Dockerfiles for web and API: non-root user, minimal base, health check. Compose or Aspire starts DB, cache, seed and application with one command on Podman or Rancher Desktop — both from source and from published version images.

Publish commit-tagged images after merges to `preview` and version-tagged images for releases on `main`; run each version; control migration application; execute smoke tests. Hosted Preview deploys automatically; hosted Release requires approval. Hosting becomes mandatory with OPS Advanced.

Keep secrets out of Git; run secret scanning (GitHub/Azure DevOps built-in where available, or tooling such as Gitleaks). Secrets in pipeline/variable-group/Key Vault storage. Cloud deployment SHOULD use OIDC workload identity instead of long-lived keys.
Scan dependencies, source (static analysis) and container images. No unresolved Critical/High finding enters a release unless a documented exception exists.
Automate weekly releases: release-PR template, semantic version tags, generated release notes/CHANGELOG, and a release record containing images, notes and (when hosted) the deployment.
Operational runbook: local setup, environments/URLs, deployment/rollback, reset/reseed, backup/restore, common failures and remediation.
Bicep for every cloud resource; parameterised per environment; deployed through the pipeline; drift detection.
An ephemeral environment per PR with seed data and automatic teardown (or revision-style previews); its URL is posted to the PR.
OpenTelemetry exported to monitoring; dashboards for latency, errors, saturation and jobs; at least 2 alerts; an incident drill with a blameless postmortem.
Blue-green or canary progressive delivery; automatic rollback on failed smoke tests; feature flags for unfinished features.
Scheduled load tests on Preview with tracked releases; a DAST baseline scan (for example OWASP ZAP); a dependency/cache chaos test with documented observed behaviour.

An SBOM for each release; pinned action/task versions; automated dependency updates with merge rules; budget alerts; scale-to-zero/auto-shutdown for non-release environments. Image signing/provenance SHOULD be used.
Use a modular monolith, or justify a different architecture in an ADR. Microservices give no scoring advantage.
Clear separation of presentation, API/application use cases, domain, persistence, cross-cutting functions, and integrations/adapters.
Backend/domain code owns business rules: state machines, billing, lease overlap, authorization relationships.
The frontend/web app accesses persistent data only through the API, including server-side frontend code.
Never put access tokens in `localStorage` or `sessionStorage`; use secure HttpOnly/SameSite cookies, directly or via a BFF.
Document C4 context/container/component architecture, deployment architecture, the data model and the Scenario A sequence. Diagrams SHOULD be maintained as code (for example Mermaid or PlantUML).
Produce at least 6 ADRs: frontend framework, API style, database, auth, caching, hosting/deployment. Every participant authors at least one.
Document API conventions: naming, versions, pagination, filtering/sorting, errors, ETag/idempotency headers, dates, money.
Decide and justify whether background jobs and real-time processing run in the API host or in a worker container.

Use Microsoft products, OSI-licensed open source, or the approved source-available exceptions only. Other commercial, source-available or company-size-threshold licences are prohibited. Check exact dependency versions and licences; list principal dependencies and licences in the README.

Create and maintain a threat model with a data-flow diagram and a STRIDE-style analysis (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege), covering principal threats and mitigations. Update it as the system changes; include the final version in the submission.
evidence: Final threat model in `docs/security/` matching the final architecture

requirement: Authentication uses secure password storage from ASP.NET Core Identity or the chosen identity provider. Account lockout or throttling. Define session and token lifetimes explicitly. Secure cookie flags. Sign-out invalidates the session. Tokens never in `localStorage`/`sessionStorage`; use HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies, directly or via a BFF. No fixed lifetime, timeout, lockout count or throttle number is prescribed — choose and document them.
evidence: Auth config/code; documented lifetimes and rationale; lockout config; cookie config; sign-in/sign-out/session-invalidation tests; storage check; auth ADR

requirement: Authorization is deny by default. Every endpoint performs object-level checks on role AND relationship to the resource. Generate automated authorization tests from the permissions matrix, including IDOR attempts (changing an ID to reach another user's records).
evidence: Policy/resource-handler code; matrix-based test suite; negative tests; cross-resident IDOR tests; manager cannot reach unassigned buildings

requirement: Validate all input on the server. Parameterized queries only. Encode output. Sanitize rich text on the server with an allow list. Configure a Content Security Policy (normally the `Content-Security-Policy` header).
evidence: Validators + tests; parameterized-access evidence; sanitizer config + malicious-input tests; CSP config

requirement: CSRF protection whenever cookies authenticate API requests (antiforgery tokens and/or SameSite cookies plus origin checks). CORS restricted to explicitly known origins; no unrestricted origins for credentialed calls.
evidence: Antiforgery/SameSite/origin config; per-environment CORS allow-list; tests that an unauthorized origin is denied

requirement: HTTPS everywhere except local development. Configure HSTS, Content-Security-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy and CSP `frame-ancestors`.
evidence: Deployment/middleware config; header test on Preview/Release; HTTP redirected or unavailable

requirement: Uploads: allow-listed file types; verify actual content (not the filename extension or client MIME type); size limits; randomized storage names; store outside the web root or in blob storage; downloads via an authorized endpoint or short-lived signed URL; images SHOULD be re-encoded or metadata-stripped (for example with SkiaSharp). Product limit for maintenance requests: up to 3 photos; example types JPEG, PNG, WebP; example limit 5 MB per photo (worked example rejects a 12 MB image: "each photo must be 5 MB or smaller"). If your enforced limit differs from the 5 MB example, document it.
evidence: Upload validation code/tests (extension/content mismatch, disallowed type, oversized, malformed); randomized names; authorization tests for downloads; signed-URL expiry config

requirement: No secrets in source control or container images. Secret scanning per OPS-C06 (GitHub/Azure DevOps scanning with push protection where available; otherwise Gitleaks as pre-commit hook and CI step). Secrets in pipeline secrets, variable groups or Key Vault. Document a rotation procedure; rotate any leaked secret immediately. Cloud deployments SHOULD use OIDC workload-identity federation, not long-lived keys.
evidence: Full-history secret scan; scanner settings; CI scan; image inspection; redacted secret-store config; written rotation procedure. "No secrets anywhere in repository history" is a BLOCKING item.

requirement: Scan dependencies and container images in CI (OPS-C07 adds static analysis). Example tools: Dependabot, `dotnet list package --vulnerable`, `npm audit`, CodeQL, .NET analyzers, ESLint security rules, Trivy, Microsoft Defender for Cloud. Before a release all Critical and High findings are fixed or covered by a documented exception.
evidence: CI workflow; scan outputs; release history; zero unresolved Critical/High or an exceptions log (risk, justification, mitigation, owner, review status)

requirement: Never log passwords, tokens, complete personal data or uploaded file contents; mask personal data that must appear. Log and audit security-relevant events (failed sign-ins, permission denials, role changes).
evidence: Structured-log samples with correlation IDs and no sensitive values; masking config; audit entries for those events

requirement: Client-facing errors are generic: RFC 9457 ProblemDetails with a correlation ID. Internal details and stack traces only in protected logs.
evidence: Central exception handler; ProblemDetails examples/tests; no stack traces/SQL/paths/secrets in responses; matching log entry via correlation ID

requirement: Rate limiting on the sign-in endpoint (Core). If BE-A06 is in scope, also on password reset and all abuse-prone endpoints, returning HTTP 429 with `Retry-After`. No requests-per-minute/burst/lockout number is prescribed — choose, document and test one.
evidence: Rate-limiter config + rationale; threshold test; 429 + `Retry-After` evidence; normal traffic unaffected

requirement: Privacy by design (GDPR mindset). Synthetic data only. Minimise personal data; document every personal field with its purpose. Residents can view their personal data.
